questions.stem: A 67 year old man has a 9 month history of cramping pain in his right calf after walking about 200 yards, relieved within minutes by standing still. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day. The right femoral pulse is palpable but the popliteal and foot pulses are absent. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 152/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely to be diseased?
questions.e: Calf claudication with a palpable femoral but absent popliteal pulse points to superficial femoral artery disease, the most common site.

steps.x: A site question: the muscle that hurts is just below the diseased artery.

clues: cramping pain in his right calf
femoral pulse is palpable but the popliteal and foot pulses are absent
steps.x: **Calf** pain + pulses lost below the femoral.

elim: Aorto-iliac disease causes buttock and thigh pain and weak femoral pulses.
Causes TIA or stroke, not leg pain.
An upper limb artery.
Causes hypertension and renal impairment.

steps.x: **E. Superficial femoral artery.** Calf claudication = superficial femoral artery; buttock = iliac.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has pain in her left calf that comes on after walking 150 yards and goes when she stands still for 2 minutes. She does not need to sit or bend forward for relief, and uphill walking makes it come on sooner. Her left foot pulses are weak. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Cramping calf pain after a set distance, relieved by standing still, with weak pulses is intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease.

steps.x: A diagnosis question: arterial or neurogenic claudication?

clues: goes when she stands still for 2 minutes
does not need to sit or bend forward
steps.x: Fixed distance, relieved by **standing still**, worse uphill, weak pulses.

elim: DVT gives constant calf pain and swelling, not exertional pain.
Neurogenic claudication is relieved by sitting or bending forward, and is easier uphill.
Joint pain, worse with weight-bearing, not a fixed walking distance.
Shooting pain down the leg, not related to a fixed distance.

steps.x: **B. Intermittent claudication.** Arterial claudication: fixed distance, relieved by standing still.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man with known peripheral arterial disease attends the vascular clinic. He has calf claudication at 100 yards. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and has hypertension. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 156/90 mmHg. The doctor inspects and palpates both legs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the affected leg?
o: Haemosiderin staining of the gaiter area
questions.e: Chronic ischaemia causes reduced or absent pulses, cold limbs, shiny skin, hair loss and ulcers.

steps.x: A finding question: arterial or venous signs?
Chronic **arterial** insufficiency: think trophic changes.

elim: A sign of chronic venous disease.
A sign of chronic venous disease.
Suggests heart failure or venous disease.
The opposite of chronic arterial insufficiency.

steps.x: **A. Cool, shiny, hairless skin.** PAD exam: weak pulses, cold, shiny, hairless skin, ulcers.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has a 1 year history of aching in both calves after walking 300 yards, relieved by rest. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and smoked for 40 years until last year. Her foot pulses are weak bilaterally. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 158/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying pathology?
questions.e: Peripheral arterial disease is atherosclerosis of the peripheral arteries, driven by smoking, diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia.

steps.x: A pathology question.

clues: after walking 300 yards, relieved by rest
type 2 diabetes, hypertension and smoked for 40 years
steps.x: Classic **atherosclerotic** risk factors with claudication.

elim: Affects young male heavy smokers.
Causes aching and swelling on standing, not exertional pain with weak pulses.
A vasculitis with systemic features.
Affects fingers and toes with colour change in the cold.

steps.x: **A. Atherosclerosis of the leg arteries.** PAD = atherosclerosis of the peripheral arteries.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with peripheral arterial disease has had burning pain in his right foot every night for 3 weeks. It wakes him and is not relieved by co-codamol. His foot is cold and pale with no palpable pulses. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 148/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which additional feature is he most likely to describe?
o: Pain that is worse when the leg hangs down
Relief by elevating the leg on pillows
Relief by hanging the leg over the side of the bed
Swelling that is worst in the evening
questions.e: Critical limb ischaemia gives rest pain worse at night when the leg is elevated, relieved by dangling the leg off the bed.

steps.x: A finding question: what eases ischaemic rest pain?
Night rest pain **>2 weeks**, unrelieved by analgesia = **critical limb ischaemia**.

elim: Venous and inflammatory pain worsen with dependency; ischaemic pain improves.
Elevation worsens ischaemic rest pain.
A feature of venous disease.
Suggests peripheral neuropathy.

steps.x: **C. Relief by hanging the leg over the side of the bed.** CLI pain is relieved by dangling the leg.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman who does not have diabetes has had rest pain in her left foot for 2 months. Her second and third toes are now black, dry and shrivelled with a clear line of demarcation. There are no palpable foot pulses. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 152/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Critical limb ischaemia with dry gangrene
questions.e: Progression from claudication to rest pain, then tissue death: resting flow is inadequate, causing gangrene.

steps.x: A diagnosis question about tissue loss in PAD.

clues: rest pain in her left foot for 2 months
steps.x: Rest pain **plus tissue loss**.

elim: Follows cold exposure, not chronic rest pain.
She does not have diabetes, and neuropathic ulcers are painless.
Causes reversible colour change, not gangrene with absent pulses.
Venous ulcers are at the medial malleolus with pulses present.

steps.x: **A. Critical limb ischaemia with dry gangrene.** CLI = rest pain >2 weeks, ulcers or gangrene.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with known claudication of his left calf has a 2 hour history of sudden severe pain in his left leg. The leg is white and very cold, he has pins and needles in his foot and he cannot move his toes. No pulses are felt below the groin. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis and perishing cold are the 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis question: acute or chronic ischaemia?

clues: 2 hour history of sudden severe pain
steps.x: **Sudden** onset with all 6 Ps.

elim: CLI is chronic rest pain over weeks, not a sudden onset over hours.
Causes a warm, swollen leg with pulses present.
Causes calf swelling with normal pulses.
Claudication only occurs on exertion and does not cause paralysis.

steps.x: **A. Acute limb ischaemia.** 6 Ps over hours = acute limb ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a 6 month history of cramp in his right calf after walking 100 yards. He smokes and has hypercholesterolaemia. He has no buttock pain or erectile dysfunction. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 144/84 mmHg. The doctor palpates the pulses of the right leg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding?
o: Palpable femoral pulse with absent popliteal and foot pulses
questions.e: Calf claudication arises from superficial femoral artery disease: the femoral pulse is felt, but pulses below are lost.

steps.x: A finding question: predict the pulses from the site of pain.

clues: no buttock pain or erectile dysfunction
steps.x: Calf, not buttock: disease is in the **femoral** segment, below the groin.

elim: Suggests aorto-iliac disease with buttock pain and impotence.
An upper limb finding.
Not consistent with arterial disease.
Suggests a muscular or venous cause.

steps.x: **E. Palpable femoral pulse with absent popliteal and foot pulses.** SFA disease: femoral present, popliteal and pedal absent.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man with peripheral arterial disease and rest pain has a painful ulcer on his right foot. It is small, deep and punched out with a pale base. The surrounding skin is cool and hairless and the foot pulses are absent. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 150/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the ulcer?
o: Plantar surface under the metatarsal heads
questions.e: Arterial ulcers of critical limb ischaemia are painful, punched-out and occur distally at the toe tips and pressure points.

steps.x: A finding question about the ulcer site.
Painful, punched-out, pulseless: an **arterial** ulcer, in the most distal skin.

elim: Not a typical site for an arterial ulcer.
Typical of venous ulcers.
Typical of painless neuropathic ulcers.
Not a typical ulcer site.

steps.x: **E. Tip of the toes.** Arterial ulcers: toe tips and pressure points.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has had claudication of her left calf at 200 yards for 3 years. She is reviewed by her GP who wants to know whether her disease has progressed and needs urgent vascular referral. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which finding would most indicate progression to critical limb ischaemia?
o: Ankle swelling at the end of the day
Calf pain now coming on at 150 yards
Ischaemic pain at rest for more than 2 weeks
Pain relieved by sitting and bending forward
questions.e: Critical limb ischaemia means ischaemic rest pain for more than 2 weeks, often at night, or ulcers and gangrene.

steps.x: A finding question about severity.

clues: claudication of her left calf at 200 yards for 3 years
steps.x: The line between claudication and CLI is **rest pain >2 weeks** or tissue loss.

elim: Suggests venous disease or a calcium channel blocker.
A shorter walking distance is worsening claudication, not CLI.
A feature of spinal stenosis.
A venous problem.

steps.x: **C. Ischaemic pain at rest for more than 2 weeks.** CLI = rest pain >2 weeks, ulcers or gangrene.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has calf claudication at 150 yards. He has type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 58 mmol/mol, treated hypertension with BP 138/82 mmHg, and a cholesterol of 5.4 mmol/L. He smokes 25 cigarettes a day. He asks which of his risk factors matters most. His pulse rate is 74 bpm.
questions.q: Which is his most important risk factor?
questions.e: Smoking is the most important risk factor for peripheral arterial disease, ahead of diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia.

steps.x: A risk factor question with several candidates.

clues: which of his risk factors matters most
steps.x: Several risks are present; one dominates in PAD.

elim: A risk factor, but less important than smoking.
A risk factor, and well controlled here.
Not modifiable and less important than smoking.
A strong risk factor, but smoking is the most important.

steps.x: **D. Smoking.** PAD: smoking is the most important risk factor.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has a 4 month history of cramp in her left calf on walking 100 yards, relieved by rest. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 150/90 mmHg. Her ankle-brachial pressure index is measured (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease
questions.e: Exertional calf cramp relieved by rest with an ABPI of 0.62 is claudication from moderate peripheral arterial disease.

steps.x: A diagnosis question with an ABPI.

clues: cramp in her left calf on walking 100 yards, relieved by rest
steps.x: The ABPI is **below 0.9**: arterial disease.

elim: The ABPI is low, which points to arterial disease.
Causes numbness and burning, not exertional cramp.
A cause of claudication in young athletes.
Bursting pain after DVT, with a normal ABPI.

steps.x: **A. Intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease.** Claudication + ABPI <0.9 = PAD.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has calf claudication at 150 yards. His ABPI is 0.64 on the right. He is keen to know where the narrowing is. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 148/88 mmHg. His eGFR is 72 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line imaging investigation?
questions.e: After ABPI, duplex ultrasound is the first-line imaging, confirming and locating the disease.

steps.x: A first-line imaging question.
ABPI confirms PAD; the next step is the **first imaging** test.

elim: Invasive; reserved for intervention.
Third-line, for more anatomical detail.
Used to plan intervention, not as the first imaging.
Does not show the arterial lumen.

steps.x: **D. Duplex ultrasound.** PAD: ABPI, then duplex ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman who smokes has mild calf discomfort on walking long distances. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm. Her brachial systolic pressure is 140 mmHg and her right ankle systolic pressure is 119 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of her ABPI?
questions.e: 119 divided by 140 is 0.85, which falls in the 0.8 to 0.9 band: mild PAD.

steps.x: An interpretation question: calculate the ratio first.
Ankle over brachial: **119/140 = 0.85**.

elim: Needs an ABPI above 1.23.
Moderate disease is 0.5 to 0.8.
Normal is 1.0 to 1.2.
Severe disease is below 0.5.

steps.x: **B. Mild peripheral arterial disease.** ABPI 0.8 to 0.9 = mild PAD.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has disabling claudication at 50 yards despite supervised exercise, clopidogrel and atorvastatin. Duplex ultrasound shows a short iliac stenosis. The vascular team plans angioplasty. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 140/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before intervention?
questions.e: CT angiography is used to image the arteries before intervention, to plan angioplasty or bypass.

steps.x: A pre-intervention investigation question.
An intervention is planned: the team needs a **road map**.

elim: Confirms PAD but gives no anatomy.
Not an imaging test for the leg arteries.
Assesses risk, not anatomy.
Assesses the veins, not the arteries.

steps.x: **B. CT angiography.** CT angiography before intervention.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has claudication and an ABPI of 0.6. Duplex ultrasound is inconclusive because of her body habitus. The vascular team needs further anatomical detail to decide whether revascularisation is possible. She has no pacemaker or metal implants and her eGFR is 68 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: When duplex is not enough, contrast-enhanced MR angiography gives further anatomical detail (CT angiography if MRA is unsuitable or to plan intervention).

steps.x: A next investigation question after duplex.
Duplex failed and **MRI is safe** for her.

elim: Already confirms disease and gives no anatomy.
Measures walking distance, not anatomy.
Does not show the arterial lumen.
Looks at the heart.

steps.x: **B. Contrast-enhanced MR angiography.** PAD imaging: duplex, then contrast MRA, CTA before intervention.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man is diagnosed with peripheral arterial disease after presenting with calf claudication. His ABPI is 0.72. He is overweight and has not seen a doctor for 10 years. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/90 mmHg. The GP wants to assess his overall cardiovascular risk.
questions.q: Which additional blood tests are most appropriate?
questions.e: Lipids and HbA1c assess hyperlipidaemia and diabetes, the treatable risk factors behind atherosclerosis.

steps.x: An additional investigation question.

clues: not seen a doctor for 10 years
steps.x: Look for **diabetes** and **hyperlipidaemia**.

elim: Not relevant to cardiovascular risk.
Not part of cardiovascular risk assessment.
Not relevant to PAD risk.
Not part of the cardiovascular risk work-up.

steps.x: **C. Lipid profile and HbA1c.** PAD bloods: lipids and HbA1c.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman has calf pain on walking 50 yards and pain in her toes at night for the last week. She smokes. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 162/92 mmHg. Her ABPI is measured (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of this result?
questions.e: An ABPI below 0.5 indicates severe peripheral arterial disease, consistent with early rest pain.

steps.x: An interpretation question using the ABPI bands.

clues: pain in her toes at night
steps.x: ABPI **0.42** is below 0.5.

elim: Gives a falsely high ABPI above 1.23.
Mild is 0.8 to 0.9.
Moderate is 0.5 to 0.8.
Normal is 1.0 to 1.2.

steps.x: **E. Severe peripheral arterial disease.** ABPI <0.5 = severe PAD.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has calf claudication at 200 yards. ABPI is 0.74. She has stopped smoking and takes clopidogrel and atorvastatin. She wants to improve her walking distance. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate exercise advice?
o: Supervised exercise 2 hours a week for 3 months
Supervised exercise 30 minutes a week for 2 weeks
Swimming only, avoiding any leg pain
questions.e: First-line for claudication is supervised exercise, about 2 hours a week for 3 months, which promotes collateral vessels.

steps.x: A management question about exercise.
First-line for claudication: a **supervised** programme.

elim: Rest worsens deconditioning and does not improve claudication.
Too infrequent and unsupervised.
Too little and too short to promote collaterals.
Exercise to near-maximal pain is the aim.

steps.x: **C. Supervised exercise 2 hours a week for 3 months.** Supervised exercise: 2 h/week for 3 months.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man is diagnosed with intermittent claudication. ABPI is 0.7. He already takes aspirin 75 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg, started 5 years ago after a GP health check. He has no history of bleeding. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change to his medication?
o: Switch to clopidogrel 75 mg and increase atorvastatin to 80 mg
questions.e: Symptomatic PAD is treated with clopidogrel 75 mg once daily and high-dose atorvastatin 80 mg (NICE CG147).

steps.x: A medication question: compare his drugs with first-line therapy.
PAD drugs: **clopidogrel 75 mg** and **atorvastatin 80 mg**.

elim: Anticoagulation is not used for stable claudication.
He needs clopidogrel and high-dose statin for PAD.
Statins reduce cardiovascular risk and slow atherosclerosis.
Clopidogrel is the antiplatelet of choice in PAD.

steps.x: **E. Switch to clopidogrel 75 mg and increase atorvastatin to 80 mg.** PAD = clopidogrel 75 mg + atorvastatin 80 mg.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with claudication at 150 yards has started a supervised exercise programme, clopidogrel and atorvastatin. His BP is 132/80 mmHg and his HbA1c is normal. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and has a BMI of 26 kg/m². His pulse rate is 76 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most important additional intervention?
o: Elevation of the legs at night
questions.e: Smoking is the most important risk factor; stopping is central to cardiovascular risk management alongside exercise, antiplatelets and statins.

steps.x: A risk management question.
Everything else is treated; one big risk factor remains.

elim: Reduce arterial flow and are contraindicated in significant PAD.
Worsens ischaemic symptoms.
Only considered if supervised exercise has not helped; stopping smoking matters far more.
Not indicated for stable PAD.

steps.x: **D. Smoking cessation support.** In PAD, stopping smoking matters most.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has severe left calf claudication at 30 yards despite 3 months of supervised exercise, clopidogrel and atorvastatin. He has COPD and ischaemic heart disease and is a high anaesthetic risk. CT angiography shows a short-segment stenosis of the superficial femoral artery. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with or without stent
questions.e: A high-risk patient with a short-segment stenosis who has failed conservative treatment is treated endovascularly with angioplasty ± stent.

steps.x: A management question: open or endovascular?
Failed conservative + **high risk** + **short segment** = endovascular.

elim: The limb is not threatened and has no tissue loss.
Conservative treatment has failed and he is disabled.
Suited to low-risk patients with long-segment disease.
Not standard treatment for claudication.

steps.x: **E. Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with or without stent.** Short segment, high risk = angioplasty ± stent.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has disabling claudication despite supervised exercise and best medical therapy. She is otherwise fit with a low operative risk. CT angiography shows long-segment, multifocal occlusion of the superficial femoral artery with good run-off below the knee. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Low-risk patients with long-segment or multifocal disease are best treated with open surgical revascularisation (bypass graft).

steps.x: A definitive management question.
**Long, multifocal** disease in a **fit** patient.

elim: The limb is viable without tissue loss.
Best for short-segment disease in high-risk patients.
Already tried and failed.
For acute thrombosis, not chronic occlusion.

steps.x: **B. Open surgical bypass graft.** Long segment, low risk = open bypass.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has severe left thigh and calf claudication despite exercise and best medical therapy. CT angiography shows occlusion of the left external iliac artery extending to the proximal common femoral artery. The right iliac system is normal. He is fit for surgery. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate operation?
questions.e: Left external iliac and proximal femoral disease is bypassed with an ilio-femoral graft (oblique iliac and vertical groin incisions).

steps.x: An operation choice question.

clues: left external iliac artery extending to the proximal common femoral artery
steps.x: Disease from the **iliac** to the **femoral**: bypass between them.

elim: The limb is viable.
For carotid stenosis.
Bypasses disease below the knee, not the iliac segment.
Not standard treatment.

steps.x: **D. Ilio-femoral bypass.** External iliac/proximal femoral disease = ilio-femoral bypass.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with known peripheral arterial disease sees her GP with 3 weeks of pain in her right foot at night that is not helped by paracetamol or codeine. She sleeps in a chair. There is a small ulcer on her heel. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 152/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase analgesia and review in 3 months
Routine referral to a vascular clinic
questions.e: Rest pain over 2 weeks with tissue loss is critical limb ischaemia, which needs urgent vascular referral.

steps.x: A next step question in primary care.

clues: 3 weeks of pain in her right foot at night
steps.x: Rest pain **>2 weeks** + ulcer + sleeping upright = **CLI**.

elim: Compression worsens arterial ischaemia.
Delay risks limb loss.
Critical limb ischaemia needs urgent assessment.
For claudication, not rest pain with tissue loss.

steps.x: **E. Urgent referral to vascular surgery.** CLI = urgent vascular referral.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man with critical limb ischaemia of the right leg has gangrene of the forefoot that is wet and foul-smelling, with cellulitis spreading to the ankle. Vascular imaging shows no vessel suitable for reconstruction. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. The knee and thigh skin are healthy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Irreversible critical limb ischaemia with superimposed infection, and no revascularisation option, is treated with below-knee amputation.

steps.x: A management question in end-stage disease.

clues: knee and thigh skin are healthy
steps.x: **Irreversible** + **infected** + **unreconstructable**; the knee is healthy.

elim: Not a treatment for unreconstructable, infected gangrene.
Infected irreversible tissue needs removing.
There is no vessel suitable for revascularisation.
For claudication only.

steps.x: **A. Below-knee amputation.** Infected irreversible CLI = below-knee amputation.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has cramp in his left calf after walking 150 yards that goes after 2 minutes of rest. His left popliteal and foot pulses are absent. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. He asks why the pain stops when he rests.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his symptoms?
o: Compression of the L5 nerve root on walking
Lactic acid from muscle overuse in normal arteries
Narrowed arteries cannot meet the oxygen demand of exercising muscle
questions.e: A plaque narrows the artery so flow cannot rise with exercise; the muscle becomes ischaemic, and pain settles when demand falls at rest.

steps.x: A mechanism question about claudication.
Supply is fixed; **demand** rises with walking and falls with rest.

elim: That is neurogenic claudication.
His pulses are absent; the arteries are narrowed.
Thrombi do not form and dissolve with each walk.
That is venous claudication after DVT.

steps.x: **C. Narrowed arteries cannot meet the oxygen demand of exercising muscle.** Claudication = supply cannot meet exercise demand.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman with critical limb ischaemia has constant burning pain in her left foot, worst when she lies flat in bed and eased when she hangs her leg over the side. Her foot pulses are absent and ABPI is 0.38. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 150/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her pain at rest?
o: Gout crystal deposition in the foot
Nerve damage from vitamin B12 deficiency
Resting blood flow is too low to meet the tissue's needs
questions.e: In CLI flow is inadequate even at rest, causing continuous ischaemic pain; dangling the leg uses gravity to increase perfusion pressure.

steps.x: A mechanism question about rest pain.

clues: eased when she hangs her leg over the side
steps.x: ABPI **<0.5** and pain at **rest**: supply fails even without exercise.

elim: Gout causes a hot, swollen joint.
Causes symmetrical neuropathy, not positional pain.
That is Raynaud's.
Venous pain worsens when the leg hangs down.

steps.x: **C. Resting blood flow is too low to meet the tissue's needs.** CLI = resting flow inadequate -> rest pain, ulcers, gangrene.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has had type 2 diabetes for 25 years. He has calf pain on walking 100 yards. His foot pulses are very faint and his toes are cool. His ABPI is 1.45 on both sides. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg. The registrar says the ABPI cannot be trusted.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason the ABPI is unreliable?
o: Brachial artery stenosis lowering arm pressure
Calcified ankle arteries cannot be compressed by the cuff
Excess subcutaneous fat at the ankle
questions.e: Diabetes calcifies the arterial wall, so the ankle vessels resist compression and the ABPI is falsely high (above 1.23).

steps.x: A science question explaining a test result.
**Diabetes** + ABPI **>1.23** + clinical PAD.

elim: Would affect the arm, and he has no arm symptoms.
Fat does not raise the ABPI this much.
Diabetes does not cause high output.
His pulses are faint and toes cool: arterial disease is likely.

steps.x: **B. Calcified ankle arteries cannot be compressed by the cuff.** ABPI >1.23 in diabetes = calcified, non-compressible arteries.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with intermittent claudication at 200 yards has an ABPI of 0.71. She has stopped smoking and has been referred for supervised exercise. She is started on clopidogrel 75 mg once daily and atorvastatin 80 mg. She asks how the clopidogrel works. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of clopidogrel?
o: Blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor
questions.e: Clopidogrel blocks the P2Y12 ADP receptor on platelets, reducing aggregation and cardiovascular events in PAD.

steps.x: A drug action question.
Clopidogrel is an **antiplatelet**, not an anticoagulant.

elim: That is heparin.
That is apixaban or rivaroxaban.
That is a statin.
That is aspirin.

steps.x: **B. Blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor.** Clopidogrel = P2Y12 blocker; reduces CV risk in PAD.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with peripheral arterial disease has a total cholesterol of 4.1 mmol/L. He is started on atorvastatin 80 mg and asks why he needs it when his cholesterol is normal. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the main reason for starting the statin?
o: To reduce cardiovascular risk and slow atherosclerosis
questions.e: High-dose statins reduce cardiovascular events and slow atherosclerotic progression in all patients with PAD, whatever the cholesterol.

steps.x: A drug rationale question.
PAD is **atherosclerosis**: the statin treats the process, not the number.

elim: Statins stabilise rather than dissolve plaques.
Not the mechanism of benefit.
Statins do not treat hypertension.
Not the indication in PAD.

steps.x: **E. To reduce cardiovascular risk and slow atherosclerosis.** Statins in PAD reduce CV risk and slow atherosclerosis.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman with calf claudication completes a 3 month supervised exercise programme. Her walking distance before pain rises from 100 yards to 350 yards. A repeat duplex ultrasound shows the superficial femoral artery stenosis is unchanged. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her improvement?
o: Lower blood viscosity from weight loss
New collateral vessels around the stenosis
questions.e: Supervised exercise promotes collateral vessel formation, improving flow around a fixed stenosis and increasing walking distance.

steps.x: A mechanism question about exercise therapy.
Same stenosis, better walking: blood is going **around** it.

elim: The duplex shows the stenosis is unchanged.
Exercise does not raise Hb enough to explain this.
Not the main mechanism.
Not the recognised mechanism.

steps.x: **D. New collateral vessels around the stenosis.** Exercise promotes collateral formation.
